items.title: 5 Mind-Blowing Facts About the Sahara Desert
items.premise: Did you know the Sahara Desert is much more than just endless sand dunes? From green historical eras to feeding the Amazon rainforest, here are 5 mind-blowing facts about the world's most famous desert.
facts: Did you know the Sahara covers 9.2 million square kilometers, making it almost the exact same size as the entire United States.
Sand dunes actually cover only 15 to 20 percent of the desert, while the rest consists of barren rocky plains and mountain ranges.
Temperatures in the Sahara can swing by over 80°F (45°C) in a single day, dropping below freezing at night.
Around 6,000 years ago, the Sahara was a lush green rainforest filled with lakes, hippos, and giraffes.
Earth's orbital tilt alters monsoon patterns every 20,000 years, periodically transforming the desert back into a green oasis.
Strong desert winds lift over 182 million tons of Saharan dust high into the atmosphere every single year.
More than 27 million tons of this nutrient-rich Saharan dust travel 3,000 miles across the Atlantic Ocean to fertilize the Amazon Rainforest.
Emi Koussi, an extinct shield volcano in Chad, forms the highest point of the Sahara at 3,415 meters (11,204 feet).
Archaeologists have discovered over 10,000 prehistoric rock carvings depicting ancient Saharan hunters and wildlife.
The Sahara spans across 11 different North African countries and continues to expand southward.

items.title: Trapped 2,300 Feet Underground: The 2010 Chilean Mine Rescue
items.premise: On August 5, 2010, 33 miners were trapped deep inside the San José gold and copper mine after a catastrophic cave-in. Against all odds, they survived 69 days underground before a historic engineering feat brought them home.
facts: On August 5, 2010, a massive 700,000-ton rock collapse trapped 33 miners inside the San José Mine near Copiapó, Chile.
The miners were trapped 700 meters (2,300 feet) underground, nearly 3 miles from the mine's entrance.
Underground shelter conditions reached 35°C (95°F) with 90 percent humidity and minimal ventilation.
With emergency food meant for only 2 days, each miner consumed just two spoonfuls of tuna every 48 hours to survive.
On August 22, 2010 (Day 17), a probe drill reached the shelter and returned to the surface with a note attached.
Written in bright red marker, the famous note read: 'Estamos bien en el refugio, los 33' ('We are well in the shelter, all 33 of us').
Engineers set up three separate drilling rigs—Plan A, Plan B, and Plan C—working around the clock to create an escape shaft.
Plan B's T130 drill successfully broke through into the underground chamber on October 9, 2010.
A custom steel rescue capsule named Fénix 2, measuring just 54 centimeters (21 inches) wide, was lowered to retrieve the men.
On October 13, 2010, after 69 days trapped underground, all 33 miners were safely brought to the surface in a 22.5-hour operation.
